title: The Law of the Sea Is in Trouble
gist: Elisabeth Braw argues the maritime duty to rescue, codified from the 1910 Brussels Convention through SOLAS and its 2004 amendments, is eroding. Far-right protesters in the UK attack RNLI crews for rescuing Channel migrants, and the US military has carried out a year-long campaign of lethal strikes on alleged drug boats, including killing survivors. She says SOLAS clearly requires aid regardless of a person's status.

insights.claim: Braw argues the US military's strikes on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Pacific violate the long-standing legal and moral obligation to save lives at sea, which the UK's RNLI still upholds.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: US erosion of maritime law norms weakens its standing to enforce freedom-of-navigation and shipping rules elsewhere.
insights.quote: today, the RNLI upholds that while the U.S. military violates it.

insights.claim: Since September 2025, US strikes on boats have repeatedly killed people, from 11 in the first Sept. 2 strike to four on Sept. 19; in one attack two survivors were killed in a second strike, and Trump has not declared the campaign over.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: An open-ended lethal maritime campaign in the Caribbean raises regional escalation risk, including with Venezuela.
insights.quote: In one infamous attack, two survivors were killed in a second strike.

insights.claim: Because the campaign targets groups Trump designates as terrorist organizations, such as TDA, which he says operates under Nicolás Maduro, Braw says it cannot end until those groups are defeated.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Framing the campaign as counterterrorism implies indefinite duration and persistent US-Venezuela tension.
insights.quote: In fact, it can’t be over, as it targets what Trump claims are terrorist organizations

insights.claim: Braw writes that the administration's legal theory that 'narcoterrorists' are combatants who may be killed at sea ignores the 2004 SOLAS and Search and Rescue amendments, which the US adopted and which require assistance regardless of nationality, status or circumstances.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
entities: International Convention on Maritime Search and Rescue
insights.so_what: Legal exposure and norm erosion could spill over into commercial shipping practice and insurance assumptions.
insights.quote: this obligation to provide assistance applies regardless of the nationality or status of such persons or the circumstances in which they are found.

insights.claim: In the UK, far-right populists have protested RNLI rescuers, tried to block buses carrying rescued Channel migrants to reception centers, and branded crews traitors online.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Points to rising anti-migrant mobilization in UK politics, a driver of policy and electoral risk.

insights.claim: SOLAS, signed in 1914 after the Titanic disaster by a small group of nations that dominated shipping, has since been updated three times and now covers 99 percent of the world's merchant vessels.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Shows how a small coalition of dominant players can set durable global standards, and why their defection matters.
insights.quote: the current version has been signed by nearly all of the world’s countries, representing 99 percent of the world’s merchant vessels.

insights.claim: Braw notes that historical precedent cuts against the US position: even the Nazis often rescued Allied seamen until 1942, and Karl Donitz escaped war-crimes charges partly because of ambiguity created by US unrestricted submarine warfare.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: US practice today may create precedents adversaries later exploit, as its WWII ambiguity once did.

insights.claim: Since 1824 RNLI volunteers have saved nearly 150,000 people, including 5,332 lives in WWI and 6,376 in WWII.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Context for the institutional depth of the UK rescue norm under political pressure.

insights.claim: Requiring rescuers to judge whether people at sea are worthy of rescue would create a moral morass, which is why SOLAS treats everyone at sea as equal.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Conditional rescue norms would raise operational and liability burdens for commercial vessel operators.
insights.quote: None of us would want nearby ships to first assess our worthiness before deciding to rescue us.
